```{python}
def join_values(values: object) -> str:
    if not isinstance(values, list) or not values:
        return reporting.NA_TEXT
    return ", ".join(str(value) for value in values)


def complete(*values: object) -> bool:
    """True when every value is present and not NaN."""
    return all(
        value is not None and not (isinstance(value, float) and math.isnan(value))
        for value in values
    )


def comparison_vintage_text(frame: pl.DataFrame | None, primary: object) -> str:
    if frame is None:
        return reporting.NA_TEXT
    values = sorted(
        {str(value) for value in frame["vintage"].to_list() if str(value) != str(primary)}
    )
    return ", ".join(values) if values else reporting.NA_TEXT


def phase2_status(frame: pl.DataFrame | None) -> str:
    if frame is None or frame.is_empty():
        return "absent"
    return "present"


P2_MT_IDS = join_values([entry.get("id") for entry in (P2_MT.get("specs") or [])])
P2_VINTAGE_PREFERENCE = join_values(P2_VINTAGES.get("compare_preference"))


def coverage_value(item: str) -> object:
    value = reporting.lookup(coverage, "value", item=item) if coverage is not None else None
    return value if value is not None else reporting.NA_TEXT


def paper_table_value(key: str) -> object:
    value = PAPER_TABLE.get(key)
    return value if value is not None else reporting.NA_TEXT


def paper_term(term: str, field: str) -> object:
    entry = PAPER_TABLE.get(term, {})
    return entry.get(field) if isinstance(entry, dict) else None


def paper_decline_pct(term: str) -> float | None:
    return reporting.ratio_pct(paper_term(term, "coef"), PAPER_IN_SAMPLE_MEAN)


def main_value(term: str, column: str) -> object:
    return reporting.lookup(main, column, term=term) if main is not None else None


def mt_lookup(spec: str, term: str, column: str) -> object:
    if multiple_testing is None:
        return None
    return reporting.lookup(multiple_testing, column, spec=spec, term=term)


def decay_value(method: str, term: str, column: str) -> object:
    if decay is None:
        return None
    return reporting.lookup(decay, column, method=method, term=term)


def pair_cell(coef: object, se: object) -> str:
    if coef is None and se is None:
        return f"*{PAPER_STATUS}*"
    if coef is None or se is None:
        return reporting.NA_TEXT
    return f"{reporting.num(coef, 3)} ({reporting.num(se, 3)})"


def callout(title: str, message: str, kind: str = "note") -> str:
    return f"::: {{.callout-{kind}}}\n## {title}\n\n{message}\n:::\n"


def note(message: str) -> str:
    return callout("Pending full-data run", message)


def render_table(
    frame: pl.DataFrame | None,
    columns: list[str],
    headers: list[str] | None = None,
    formats: dict | None = None,
    missing: str = "The results file this table reads has not been produced yet.",
    group: str | None = None,
    labels: dict | None = None,
) -> Markdown:
    if frame is None:
        return Markdown(note(missing))
    if group is not None:
        return Markdown(
            reporting.grouped_table(frame, group, columns, headers, formats, labels)
        )
    return Markdown(reporting.table(frame, columns, headers, formats))
```

# Question

Do long-short anomaly returns fall once the original sample ends, and fall further once the
research is published? McLean and Pontiff (2016) answer yes for a hand-collected sample of
`{python} paper_table_value("n_predictors")` published anomalies. Their post-sample coefficient
is `{python} reporting.num(paper_term("post_sample", "coef"), 3)` percent per month and their
post-publication coefficient is `{python} reporting.num(paper_term("post_publication", "coef"), 3)`,
against an in-sample mean of `{python} reporting.num(PAPER_IN_SAMPLE_MEAN, 3)` percent per month.
Estimated post-sample returns are `{python} reporting.direction(paper_decline_pct("post_sample"))`
than in-sample by `{python} reporting.pct(reporting.magnitude(paper_decline_pct("post_sample")))`,
and post-publication returns are
`{python} reporting.direction(paper_decline_pct("post_publication"))` by
`{python} reporting.pct(reporting.magnitude(paper_decline_pct("post_publication")))` — the
declines the paper headlines as
`{python} reporting.pct(PAPER_HEADLINE.get("post_sample_decline_pct"), 0)` and
`{python} reporting.pct(PAPER_HEADLINE.get("post_publication_decline_pct"), 0)`.

This project rebuilds that result from the open Chen–Zimmermann *Open Source Asset Pricing*
(OSAP) long-short portfolios, extends the return sample through the pinned vintage's last month
(the Data section gives the exact coverage), and adds the pre-registered
Phase 2 analyses: a moving-block bootstrap of the main decay estimates, a multiple-testing lens,
and a comparison against an earlier OSAP vintage. Like the original, the main specification asks
whether the decay is larger after publication than after the sample ends.

Returns are percent per month in both OSAP and the Ken French library, and nothing is converted.
OSAP dates are the last trading day of each month, so every join uses a `yyyymm` key, never the
raw date. Risk factors (FF5 plus momentum) come from the Ken French library, downloaded
`{python} FRENCH_DOWNLOADED_ON` and pinned in `data/pinned/`, so a fresh clone reproduces without

# Method

Each predictor-month is classified into exactly one window by year-month arithmetic:

- `in_sample` — January of the predictor's `SampleStartYear` through December of its
  `SampleEndYear`, inclusive.
- `post_sample` — the months after the sample ends and before publication.
- `post_publication` — the months from publication onward. The default convention starts in
  January of the year after the publication year, so no month is treated as published before the
  paper existed; the pre-registered alternative starts in January of the publication year. If
  publication falls inside or before the sample, `in_sample` wins and `post_sample` is empty for
  that predictor.

Pre-sample months are dropped when the panel is built, so every row used in estimation lies in
exactly one of the three windows.

The main specification pools every predictor and estimates

```text
ret = entity fixed effects + b_post_sample * post_sample + b_post_publication * post_publication + e
```

with standard errors clustered by month. Two further pre-registered covariance estimates — two-way
clustering by month and predictor, and Driscoll–Kraay with a Bartlett kernel — and the
publication-convention, sample-start, universe, portfolio and factor-adjustment variants are
reported in the robustness table. The original paper instead uses FGLS with a contemporaneous
cross-sectional correlation correction; that covariance is not reproduced here, so the standard
errors are comparable in kind but not numerically identical to the paper's.

Decay is reported two ways. The pooled ratio divides each coefficient by the pooled in-sample mean
of the same estimation sample (the paper's headline definition); the normalized regression
divides each predictor's returns by its own in-sample mean first, excludes predictors whose mean
is non-positive, and counts them in `n_predictors`. Factor-adjusted returns subtract each
predictor's FF5 plus momentum exposure — betas estimated on in-sample months only, starting from
the first month for which all of the factors exist — from every month's return; the long-short
series is zero-investment, so the risk-free rate is not subtracted.

Every specification in this report is pre-registered in `config/specifications.yaml` and frozen by
the annotated tag `specs-frozen` before the first full-data estimation; the Phase 2 analyses are
pre-registered in `config/phase2_preregistration.yaml` and frozen with it. Anything added after
the freeze must be labelled exploratory, and the appendix lists every specification with its
status.

```{python}
#| echo: false
def decline_phrase(left: object, right: object) -> str:
    word = reporting.decline_word(left, right)
    if word == "the same":
        return "is the same size as the paper's"
    return f"is {word} than the paper's"


if complete(
    main_value("post_sample", "coef"),
    main_value("post_publication", "coef"),
    repl_decay_sample,
    repl_decay_publication,
    paper_decay_sample,
    paper_decay_publication,
):
    comparison_text = Markdown(
        "The first table places the replication's main estimates beside the paper's Table II, "
        "column 1. The standard-error calculations are not the same: this replication clusters "
        "by month inside a panel regression with predictor fixed effects, while the paper's "
        "estimates allow contemporaneous cross-correlation of portfolio residuals. The "
        "replication runs on "
        f"{reporting.count(main_value('post_sample', 'n_predictors'))} predictors and "
        f"{reporting.count(main_value('post_sample', 'n_obs'))} observations against the paper's "
        f"{reporting.count(PAPER_TABLE.get('n_predictors'))} predictors and "
        f"{reporting.count(PAPER_TABLE.get('n_obs'))} observations, so the two exercises share "
        "the measured object — the shift in long-short returns after the sample ends and after "
        "publication — but not their inputs.\n\n"
        "On the pooled-ratio scale the replication's post-sample decline is "
        f"{reporting.pct(repl_decay_sample)} against the paper's implied "
        f"{reporting.pct(paper_decay_sample)}, and the post-publication decline is "
        f"{reporting.pct(repl_decay_publication)} against "
        f"{reporting.pct(paper_decay_publication)}. The gaps are "
        f"{reporting.pp_gap(repl_decay_sample, paper_decay_sample)} and "
        f"{reporting.pp_gap(repl_decay_publication, paper_decay_publication)}: the replication's "
        f"post-sample decline {decline_phrase(repl_decay_sample, paper_decay_sample)}, and its "
        "post-publication decline "
        f"{decline_phrase(repl_decay_publication, paper_decay_publication)}. In magnitude the "
        "replication's post-sample coefficient is "
        f"{reporting.factor(main_value('post_sample', 'coef'), paper_term('post_sample', 'coef'))} "
        "the paper's and its post-publication coefficient is "
        f"{reporting.factor(main_value('post_publication', 'coef'), paper_term('post_publication', 'coef'))} "
        "the paper's."
    )
else:
    comparison_text = Markdown("")
comparison_text
```

Three documented differences can move these numbers: the predictor universe (OSAP reconstructs
each signal following its original paper, where McLean and Pontiff hand-collected their returns),
the portfolio construction (`op` long-short series per signal versus the authors' own series) and
the standard-error correction. None of them changes the question or the definition of the
measured object, so the side-by-side comparison is the replication test, not an equality test on
the coefficients.

One further note on the source table: the paper prints the post-sample coefficient with three
stars, but the printed coefficient and standard error imply t =
`{python} reporting.tstat(paper_t_sample)`; the value is reproduced here exactly as printed, and
the note in `config/original_paper.yaml` records the inconsistency. The paper's values come from
`config/original_paper.yaml` (status: *`{python} PAPER_STATUS`*).

# Robustness

The pre-registered robustness rows vary the clustering (two-way, Driscoll–Kraay), the
publication convention, the later-sample-start filter, the clear-predictors-only universe,
the decile portfolios, factor-adjusted returns and normalized returns. The coefficient plot
shows each row's post-sample and post-publication coefficient with a 95% confidence
interval.

# Extension

The extension reruns the main specification on every predictor through the pinned
vintage's last month and splits the post-publication shift by publication era (the
`ext_pub_after_2000` entry of `config/specifications.yaml`), so the decay can be compared
across later and earlier literature.

```{python}
#| tbl-colwidths: [30, 20, 11, 9, 8, 11, 11]
extension_view = render_table(
    reporting.ordered(extension, {"spec": SPEC_ORDER, "term": TERM_ORDER})
    if extension is not None
    else None,
    ["spec", "term", "coef", "se", "t", "n_predictors", "n_obs"],
```

# Phase 2: Bootstrap inference

The first pre-registered Phase 2 analysis puts sampling uncertainty on the headline estimates
with a moving-block bootstrap: contiguous blocks of
`{python} reporting.count(P2_BOOTSTRAP.get("block_length_months"))` calendar months are drawn
with replacement until the estimation sample's length is reached (block method:
`{python} reporting.block_method_label(P2_BOOTSTRAP.get("method"))`), every predictor's
observations in a month move together, and the main specification is re-estimated in each of
`{python} reporting.count(P2_BOOTSTRAP.get("reps"))` replicates with seed
`{python} reporting.num(P2_BOOTSTRAP.get("seed"), 0)`. Intervals are percentile intervals at the
`{python} reporting.pct(reporting.ratio_pct(P2_BOOTSTRAP.get("level"), 1), 0)` level. The
pre-registration marks the analysis
`{python} reporting.exploratory_label(P2_BOOTSTRAP.get("exploratory"))`.

```{python}
#| tbl-colwidths: [16, 40, 12, 12, 10, 10]
BOOTSTRAP_ORDER = P2_BOOTSTRAP.get("statistics") or []
BOOTSTRAP_LABELS = {
    "coef_post_sample": "Post-sample coefficient",
    "coef_post_publication": "Post-publication coefficient",
    "decay_pct_post_sample": "Post-sample pooled-ratio decay",
    "decay_pct_post_publication": "Post-publication pooled-ratio decay",
}
bootstrap_view = render_table(
    reporting.ordered(bootstrap, {"spec": ["bootstrap_main"], "statistic": BOOTSTRAP_ORDER})
    if bootstrap is not None
    else None,
    ["spec", "statistic", "estimate", "boot_se", "ci_low", "ci_high"],
    ["Spec", "Statistic", "Estimate", "Boot SE", "Low", "High"],
    formats={
        "statistic": lambda value: BOOTSTRAP_LABELS.get(str(value), str(value)),
        **{
            column: (lambda value: reporting.num(value, 3))
            for column in ("estimate", "boot_se", "ci_low", "ci_high")
        },
    },
    missing="`bootstrap.csv` has not been produced yet; the pre-registered bootstrap intervals render here after the Phase 2 run.",
    group="spec",
    labels={"bootstrap_main": "Main"},
)
bootstrap_view
```

Coefficient statistics (`coef_post_sample`, `coef_post_publication`) are in percent per month;
the decay statistics (`decay_pct_post_sample`, `decay_pct_post_publication`) are in percent.
The `spec` column names the resampled specification, and the file's `reps`, `block_length` and
`seed` columns record the run parameters. The intervals answer how much of the headline decay
estimate is sampling noise under the pre-registered block scheme, not how the estimate was
selected.

# Phase 2: Multiple-testing lens

The second pre-registered analysis asks whether predictors with weaker original evidence decay
more. A predictor counts as *weak* when its t statistic is strictly below the pre-registered
hurdle of `{python} reporting.num(P2_MT.get("hurdle_t"), 1)` (the hurdle Harvey, Liu and Zhu
suggest for newly claimed factors); missing t statistics are
`{python} reporting.missing_tstat_label(P2_MT.get("missing_tstat"))` and are never imputed. Two
sources are used: the t statistic reported in the OSAP signal documentation (`original_paper` in
the results file), and the t statistic of the `op` long-short return over the predictor's own
in-sample months, computed from the same data as this replication (`in_sample_replicated`).

```{python}

    "original_paper": "Original paper",
    "in_sample_replicated": "Replicated in-sample",
}
tstat_summary_view = render_table(
    reporting.ordered(tstat_summary, {"tstat_source": TSTAT_ORDER})
    if tstat_summary is not None
    else None,
    ["tstat_source", "n_predictors", "n_missing", "n_below_hurdle", "median_t", "hurdle_t"],
    ["Source", "N pred.", "Missing", "Below hurdle", "Median t", "Hurdle"],
    formats={
        "tstat_source": lambda value: TSTAT_LABELS.get(str(value), str(value)),
        "n_predictors": reporting.count,
        "n_missing": reporting.count,
        "n_below_hurdle": reporting.count,
        "median_t": lambda value: reporting.tstat(value),
        "hurdle_t": lambda value: reporting.num(value, 2),
    },
    missing="`tstat_summary.csv` has not been produced yet; the t-statistic counts render here after the Phase 2 run.",
)
tstat_summary_view
```

The three pre-registered specifications (`{python} P2_MT_IDS`) re-run the main sample with
interaction terms between the window indicators and the weak flag, or between the window
indicators and the continuous replicated t statistic (the analogue of McLean and Pontiff's
Table II, column 4). A negative interaction on a window term means the weak group's window shift
is more negative than the comparison group's; a positive interaction means the opposite. The
`n_weak` and `n_excluded_missing_t` columns make the composition of each estimation sample
visible.

# Deviations from the original paper

Every design difference is listed here; the comparison with the paper is interpreted subject to
all of them.

1. **Publication timing.** OSAP records a publication *year* only, not the journal cover month
   that McLean and Pontiff use. The default post-publication window therefore starts in January
   of the year after the publication year, so no month is treated as published before the paper
   existed; the pre-registered alternative (January of the publication year) is reported in the
   robustness table.
2. **Predictors and construction.** McLean and Pontiff hand-collect
   `{python} reporting.num(PAPER_TABLE.get("n_predictors"), 0)` published anomalies. This
   replication uses the predictors in the pinned OSAP release (the Data section gives the counts),
   each rebuilt by Chen and Zimmermann following the signal's original paper (`op` series) rather
   than the authors' own portfolios, so return levels differ in detail even where the signal is
   the same.
3. **Standard errors.** The main specification clusters by month inside a predictor-fixed-effects
   panel regression; the paper's Table II estimates are FGLS with a contemporaneous
   cross-sectional correlation correction. Two-way clustering and Driscoll–Kraay (Bartlett
   kernel) are pre-registered robustness rows.
4. **Sample-period granularity.** OSAP supplies sample start and end *years*, and the window
   rules apply them at year granularity. Hand-checked examples: Sloan (1996) runs 1962–1991 and
   matches; Novy-Marx (2013) runs July 1963–December 2010, so the in-sample window here starts
   six months earlier; Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) run January 1965–December 1989 while OSAP
   records 1964 as the start year — the end year, and so the post-sample boundary, agree.
5. **Return sample.** The main specification stops in December 2013 like the paper; the
   extension runs to the pinned vintage's last month (given in the Data section), and some
   option-based predictors end earlier because their inputs require listed options.
6. **Decile portfolios.** The equal- and value-weighted decile variants exist for fewer predictors
   than `op` (the counts are in the Data section): signals without a discrete sort have no decile
   portfolios, so those robustness rows use the smaller universe.
7. **Factor adjustment.** Factor-adjusted returns start in July 1963 (the first FF5 month) and use
   betas estimated on in-sample months only, with no risk-free subtraction (the long-short series
   is zero-investment); the paper's factor analysis follows a different procedure.
8. **Reproducibility.** Result files are byte-identical across runs on the same machine; across
   operating systems they agree to about 1e-13 relative because the linear-algebra libraries
   differ, and the tests compare at 1e-10.
9. **Dates.** OSAP dates are the last trading day of the month (including Saturdays before
   mid-1952); all joins use year-month keys, never the raw date.

# Limitations

- **No causal claim.** The specifications estimate shifts in average long-short returns across
  windows, not the effect of publication. Predictors can weaken for reasons unrelated to the
  research — changing arbitrage capital, trading costs, risk exposures — and neither the paper's
  design nor this one separates those channels.
- **Data revisions.** OSAP is a living dataset: this report is conditional on the pinned release
  (named in the Data section), and later releases rebuild portfolios from updated inputs. The
  pre-registered vintage comparison quantifies how much one earlier release moves the estimates
  on the predictor intersection.
- **Reconstruction differences.** OSAP rebuilds each predictor following its original paper, so
  small differences in portfolio construction, sample windows and return filters persist even for
  signals the paper also covered; the deviation list gives the hand-checked examples.
- **Multiple testing.** With the release's full predictor set, large t statistics occur by chance
  even when nothing predicts returns. The multiple-testing section reports hurdle counts and
  interaction estimates under the pre-registered scheme, but it is one lens on the evidence, not
  a correction for the full search that produced the literature.
- **Gross returns.** Returns are long-short portfolio returns before trading costs; the paper's
  question is about predictability, and costs are out of scope here.
- **Window conventions.** The publication-year convention can shift the post-publication boundary
  by up to a year relative to a journal-date convention, and the sample-year convention can move
  the start of an in-sample window by a few months (see the hand-checked examples).
- **Fixtures.** The committed *data* fixture is a real 15-predictor subset of the vintage used by
  the offline tests; the committed *results* fixture holds fictional values used only to exercise
  the report's layout. Neither is evidence, and the fixture tables are not interpreted.

# Reproduction

From a clean clone, `uv sync --frozen` installs the pinned environment. Then either

```bash
make reproduce-fixture   # offline: fixture inputs, then this report from fixture results
```

checks the toolchain without network access, or

```bash
make reproduce           # fetch -> metadata -> panel -> estimate -> descriptive -> figures -> report
```

downloads the pinned OSAP vintage into the gitignored cache, verifies every cached file
against the committed SHA-256 manifest (`data/manifest.lock`), and renders this report from
`results/`. `make verify-hashes` re-checks the cache at any time and prints
`all hashes match`.

The fixture gate is the project's offline regression test: it runs the same pipeline on a
committed development subset of the vintage's predictor files, rebuilds the panel and asserts
it is exactly equal to an independently built reference panel, compares the fixture `main.csv`
with committed expected values to a tolerance of 1e-10, requires a second run of the result
stages to leave every file byte-identical, and renders both the HTML and PDF of this document.

On one machine, rerunning `make reproduce` leaves every file under `results/` byte-identical to
the committed copy: the results CSVs are sorted by key columns with fixed float formatting, and
the figure files carry no timestamps. Across operating systems the linear-algebra libraries
differ (macOS Accelerate versus OpenBLAS on Linux), so the same computation agrees to about
1e-13 relative and the tests compare at 1e-10; the committed results were produced on macOS.
This document contains no typed result: every prose number and table cell is computed at render
time through `anomaly_decay.reporting` from the results directory (`results/` by default;
`ANOMALY_DECAY_RESULTS` overrides it, which is how the fixture gate renders this same document
from fixture results), and a results file that has not been produced yet renders a visible
pending note instead of failing the render.
